results.finding: Pacing is recommended in patients with third-degree or high-degree AV block, or second-degree Mobitz type II AV block, irrespective of symptoms, once reversible causes are excluded.
results.source: Glikson M et al., 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy. Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427-3520

results.finding: In unexplained syncope with bifascicular block, pacing is indicated when an electrophysiology study shows an HV interval of 70 ms or longer, or second- or third-degree intra- or infra-Hisian block during incremental atrial pacing.
results.source: Glikson M et al., 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy. Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427-3520

results.evidence_level: Class I, level C (symptom correlation); Class IIa, level C (asymptomatic)
results.finding: A correlation between syncope and a recorded brady- or tachyarrhythmia confirms arrhythmic syncope; without a symptom correlation, Mobitz II or third-degree AV block or a ventricular pause over 3 s on monitoring makes arrhythmic syncope likely.
results.source: Brignole M et al., 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope. Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948

general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Convulsive syncope (brief myoclonic jerks from cerebral hypoperfusion) is frequently misdiagnosed as an epileptic seizure
Trifascicular pattern (bifascicular block with first-degree AV block) on ECG is a high-risk finding that calls for inpatient monitoring
Mobitz type II AV block is infranodal and does not improve with atropine or exercise, unlike Mobitz type I, which is AV nodal
Worsening of AV block with exercise indicates infra-Hisian disease, since AV nodal conduction improves with sympathetic tone
Thiazide diuretics can cause hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, which may aggravate conduction abnormalities

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Crawford is a 62-year-old man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, and prior anterior STEMI who presents to the emergency department after his third episode of sudden loss of consciousness in approximately six weeks. He was brought in by ambulance after collapsing at a grocery store approximately 90 minutes ago. A bystander witnessed the event and reported that the patient was standing in the checkout line when he suddenly dropped to the ground without any preceding stumble or warning cry. The witness describes that after falling, the patient exhibited brief jerking movements of his arms and legs lasting approximately 10-15 seconds, then lay still and appeared pale. He regained consciousness within approximately 30-40 seconds of the onset, was immediately conversational, and asked where he was. He denied any preceding lightheadedness, chest pain, palpitations, or aura. He did not bite his tongue and there was no urinary incontinence. By the time EMS arrived approximately 8 minutes later, the patient was sitting upright and reported feeling entirely normal. His two prior episodes occurred approximately six weeks ago and three weeks ago. The first event happened while he was watching television at home; he lost consciousness without warning and his neighbor, who was visiting, noted approximately 5 seconds of bilateral arm jerking before he spontaneously recovered. He did not seek medical attention for that episode. The second event occurred while climbing stairs in his apartment building; he suddenly blacked out, fell backwards down three stairs, and sustained a left elbow abrasion. Again, no prodrome, no post-ictal confusion beyond a brief period of disorientation lasting less than one minute, and no tongue biting or incontinence. He saw his primary care physician after the second event, who referred him for neurology evaluation with concern for new-onset seizures. He was seen briefly in a neurology clinic one week ago but no EEG had yet been performed. He reports increasing fatigue and exercise intolerance over the past several months, noting that he becomes short of breath climbing one flight of stairs. He has not noticed palpitations but admits he has not been monitoring his pulse. He denies any recent medication changes, missed doses, fever, or acute illness.

CN XII: Tongue protrudes midline, no fasciculations or atrophy.
